Prior to 2025, imported SAF received a tax credit; however, imported fuel no longer qualifies. In addition to federal policy, states have introduced various mechanisms to enable SAF markets. SAF qualifies for tradeable credit values in states with Low Carbon Fuel Standards, including California, New Mexico, Oregon, and Washington. Several other states provide SAF-specific incentives: • Illinois: $1.50/gal for SAF purchased or used in the state by airline common carriers effective through Dec. 31, 2032 (Illinois Department of Revenue 2023). • Minnesota: $1.50/gal for SAF produced or blended in the state and used for flights departing Minnesota effective through July 1, 2030. There is also a sales exemption for SAF facility construction materials through July 1, 2034 (Minnesota Department of Revenue 2025). • Nebraska: $0.75/gal (up to an additional $0.50/gal for emissions reductions exceeding 50%) effective through Jan. 1, 2035 (Nebraska Farm Bureau 2024). • Washington: The following incentive is triggered if in-state SAF production reaches 20 million gallons/year and is effective for 10 years (Port of Seattle 2023): $1.00/gal (up to $2.00/gal for emissions reductions exceeding 50%) for SAF produced or blended in-state for flights departing Washington. A non-policy financial mechanism enabling the SAF market is book-and-claim, which decouples the physical location of where SAF is used from its environmental value. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Center for Transportation & Logistics in partnership with the Smart Freight Centre developed guidelines to enable book-and-claim (Massachusetts Institute of Technology 2021). The “book” refers to SAF producers’ generation of certificates (also referred to as credits) documenting a volume of SAF that was produced and consumed. The “claim” refers to the purchasers of certificates, such as airlines or corporations, who claim the emissions reductions. 2.2.3 SAF Pricing and Production Costs SAF pricing data availability is limited due to few producers and low volumes across only a select number of pathways. More robust pricing data are expected in future years when there are more producers and higher volumes. Typically, most current reports and studies state that SAF costs between 2 and 5 times more than conventional jet fuel (World Economic Forum 2024; U.K. Department for Transport 2024; Royal Aeronautical Society 2025). S&P Global collects and sells SAF pricing data. They published European SAF HEFA prices for January 2024 through September 2025 (Figure 28; Gerrish et al. 2025).
